title: Asks to repair shared Git metadata after a host reboot

source.note: Runtime facts were not recorded; the turn is assumed to have ended cleanly with nothing in flight.

messages.text:
finish implementing .agents/plans/bifrost-native-resolution-engine.md

I'm in a hurry, so parallelize what you can.

  Also: remember that builds here are SLOW, it's fucking rust and it's over 1M sloc. The more work you can reasonably get done
  between build and test cycles, the more efficient it will be, obviously there are diminishing returns in extremis so don't be
  ridiculous, just use good judgement.

hang on the two reasonable approaches are

1. let the cache upgrade finish
2. nuke the old cache and start fresh

- then parallelize with worktree-per-language-group, astra subagents (not luna!) owning each, you own merge, create worktrees in /mnt/optane/

if you agree, pls enshrine it in the execplan
is there anything we can parallelize in M2 and M3?
sounds good, make it so, worktrees in /mnt/optane as for M4 pls

so do it
Finish M2 and M3
does this represent a bug in the migration?
fix it and finish M2/M3

i don't want to waste any more time on migrations for 2771

record a decision that 2771 will start the schema fresh and make that obvious in the startup path so we can't fuck it up on merge

existing cache files will be replaced you mean

but use BIFROST_CACHE_ROOT=/mnt/optane/bifrost-cache-2771 to avoid disturbing other agents until we push to master
why were we visiting the node multiple times? did you fix it correctly/generally or just patch the symptom?
/goal finish M2/M3
publication row limit? why is that a thing?
/goal finish M2/M3, then merge origin/master into our worktree, then proceed to M4

The namespace-route and import-role fixes are integrated, and the full six-package gate is building.

The real workload also exposed a cache replacement bottleneck: it is spending CPU deleting an old source publication, not parsing. I’m checking the cascade cost without changing the cache or interrupting its transaction. This is native-generation replacement, not a pre-2771 migration.

The cache bottleneck is confirmed: deleting each semantic term scans the source’s partial paths again. For one source, that means hundreds of millions of row visits.

I’m fixing the missing foreign-key indexes and adding a deletion-cost regression. I’ll stop this diagnostic retry while that fix is prepared; completed cache publications will remain in place.

The full gate passed 5,275 of 5,289 tests. The remaining failures cover import/rename consistency, an unrelated-module completeness leak, and outdated fixture or work-budget expectations.

The deletion fix is also being checked against actual deletes. That caught an important detail: SQLite’s foreign-key checks ignored the proposed partial indexes before statistics were collected, so those indexes would not reliably fix the bottleneck.

The row limit is a batching target, not a valid reason to reject a large source file; that distinction is now fixed. The next bottleneck is separate: replacing native facts triggers expensive foreign-key scans. We’ve identified the index shape SQLite actually uses and are checking that deletion scales linearly before rebuilding.

I’ve also integrated a resolver fix that shares module-route checks across names and namespaces and skips closure checks when an exact bridge already exists. The validation batch will cover that, the import/rename corrections, and the foreign-key indexes together; I’m not increasing the work budget to mask repeated work.

The replacement fix is now in the combined build. In the diagnostic fixture, doubling native rows now roughly doubles deletion work, instead of nearly quadrupling it. The indexes add about 11% to that fixture’s publication work; I’m checking the tradeoff against the bundled SQLite tests before retrying the real cache.

The focused run passed 178 of 181 tests, including native deletion/rollback, scoped usages, and rename. The three failures are in the test checks: one schema audit mishandles expression indexes, and two work/cancellation measurements need updating. Another worker has finished removing a per-bridge reference rescan; I’m reviewing that for the next batch.

The full six-package gate is running again. The bridge compiler now uses exact route-key lookups instead of comparing every bridge with every reference. I’m also removing unnecessary index construction from the normal scoped path while that gate runs.

The broader run found the remaining budget problem: bounded callers were still using the old full-scan bridge compiler. That path now uses the indexed compiler, without raising the budget. It also caught a query-planner regression from one new index; I’m checking that before treating the storage change as validated.

The full run finished at 5,287/5,293 passing. The remaining failures are the budget path, a planner regression, and stale test expectations. The real-cache diagnostic is still building the new native indexes in the dedicated cache; it is progressing, and I’m leaving it running while I finish those corrections.

The real cache has passed the former replacement stall: the base and target updates published all 10 required blobs, about two million rows, with no failed blobs. The next build includes the indexed caller path and removes the redundant index that disrupted ordered macro reads.

The module-system gate now passes under the unchanged budget. A later reverse-query check exposed another gap: empty namespaces were being marked incomplete even through a fully known reexport. The fix is ready for review, with transitive and diamond cases plus checks that cycles and unknown sources still remain incomplete.

The cache rebuild is now spending its time writing rows, not in the old quadratic lookup. A sampled 75-second interval completed 24 blobs and about 746,000 native row mutations, plus source rows. In parallel, a root-path read optimization has shown a 57% reduction in SQLite work on a representative page; its validation is still in progress.

The latest focused run passed 198/200 tests, including the new reexport cases. The remaining failures are the work-count expectation and the late-cancellation test probe. Their corrections are queued with the faster root reader so they can share the next build.

It’s a transaction-size target, not a limit on what can be published. Grouping writes bounds transaction size and cancellation delay; an indivisible source group larger than the target must still publish on its own. The fix removes that rejection.

I’m continuing M2/M3 validation. The hydration optimization also improves ordinary local paths, so we can use one general implementation instead of adding a root-only special case.

The latest focused run passed 198 of 200 tests. The remaining failures are a changed work-count expectation and a cancellation-phase test; corrections are queued for confirmation. The full-workspace fact refresh is still making progress in the isolated cache while I batch those corrections with the faster hydrator.

I also checked where 400,000 came from: the writer profile recorded roughly 3.5× lower commit cost with 256-blob/400k-row batches than with 64-blob/100k-row batches. That explains the batching target—but not rejecting a large file. The code now explicitly allows one complete source and its language projections to exceed it.

The cancellation review found no publication bug: answers remain local until final cancellation and selection checks pass. The test counts raw cancellation polls, including SQLite callbacks, so repeating a poll threshold need not reproduce the same phase. The revised test retains the cancellation it actually observed and still requires full baseline work with no returned answer. Runtime confirmation is next.

The general hydrator is integrated, and the full six-package gate is running with all queued corrections. The old SQL remains a test oracle; production uses the typed projection for every candidate. The cache refresh is continuing separately, so completed fact publications remain reusable.

The readiness audit found two missing M2 consumer checks: Rust native results have not yet been exercised through the actual RQL edge-rendering and relevance-ranking paths. I’m assigning those fixtures to two isolated Astra lanes now, while the current gate runs. Production routing stays unchanged.

The full run now passes the cancellation-phase checks and complete cross-crate reverse-result assertions. It exposed two further test corrections: trailing counters still described the older inventory, and the hydration benchmark had only two short local paths instead of a full page. Both corrections are committed; the run is still collecting any other failures before the next build.

The new RQL shadow fixtures are integrated: they exercise native alias references, empty decoys, incomplete inventories, and cancellation after rendering but before publication. The relevance/dead-code lane is still working. The full run has reported no additional failures so far; its long-running planner test is still pending.

The six-package run finished at 5,293/5,295, with only the two corrected test failures. Adding the RQL tests exposed test-support methods that were still gated to analysis-unit tests; I corrected those gates, and the expanded build is running. This does not change production routing.

The expanded build has passed the analysis type checks. The relevance/dead-code fixtures are in final review: they use real native results to test ranking and cache admission, plus the rule that incomplete empty usage results must not certify dead code. The isolated fact refresh is also still progressing.

The expanded run has started all 5,843 tests. It found a statistics-fixture ordering error: the new benchmark tried to run its “never analyzed” case after installing statistics for another path shape. I’m correcting that loop order, preserving both path shapes and both statistics states. No other failures have been reported yet.

Both consumer lanes are now integrated. The expanded run has reported only the statistics-ordering failure so far; the earlier point, reverse, and work-accounting failures have not recurred. The next batch will validate that correction together with the new ranking and dead-code fixtures.

The expanded gate finished at 5,842/5,843. Both new RQL tests passed, as did all the earlier consumer and work-budget corrections. The sole failure was the statistics-ordering issue, now corrected. The next run includes that fix and the newly integrated relevance/dead-code tests.
Selected model is at capacity. Please try a different model.
Continue Finish M2 and M3

Continuing. The latest broad run passed 5,842 of 5,843 tests; its sole failure is corrected, and the next run also includes the new ranking and dead-code checks. The isolated cache refresh is still progressing. Next are the scale checks and exact #2767 partition, then the atomic Rust production cutover for M3.

The cache refresh has finished: all 1,919 stored Rust interiors now use the current producer, with zero failed blobs. The diagnostic has moved on to native resolution. Its executable predates the latest resolver and hydration changes, so it will not certify the current tree, but the completed fact rebuild is reusable for the next run.

The old diagnostic exposed another repeated-scan problem in qualified-prefix continuation: each prefix still scans whole topology inventories, despite the indexed compiler used elsewhere. I’m assigning that correction now. I’ll also add subphase timing so we can separate native prefix lookup from topology continuation on the next run. No cache rebuild or producer change is needed for this fix.

The full seven-package gate is green: 5,845/5,845 tests passed, including hydration, RQL, ranking/cache admission, and incomplete dead-code evidence.

M2 still needs the scale checks and exact partition. I’m batching the confirmed prefix-index correction into the next validation cycle, while a separate read-only sample checks the running diagnostic’s reverse-query phase for another repeated-scan problem.

The reverse-query sample found another concrete duplication: cached requests share one interned completion record, but repeatedly merge its full reason set. A second lane is fixing that physical duplication while preserving per-request budget charges and cancellation evidence.

I’m stopping the obsolete diagnostic now. Its fact publications are complete and retained; the next run will use both query fixes.

While the two query fixes are being reviewed, I’m running the three scale checks against the binary from the green broad gate, avoiding another build. The indexed prefix implementation is ready for review; the completion-evidence fix is still in progress. I’ll compile them together for the next exact diagnostic.

The shared gate passed 5,845 tests. Two query-cost fixes are now ready; the scale runs also exposed outdated expectations after the resolver correctly began including import references. I’m reviewing the last fix, then I’ll validate them together before retrying the exact M2 acceptance case.

Both fixes are integrated and compiling together. Prefix resolution now reuses a per-profile index, and cached reverse reads combine each shared evidence set only once while retaining work charges and cancellation checks. The old diagnostic was stopped after its reusable facts finished; the next run will use the current code.

Compilation passed, and the full 5,848-test gate plus the scale campaigns are running from the same build. I’m also using this interval for read-only M3 preparation, so the production cutover can start promptly once M2’s exact result is accepted.

All three scale campaigns passed at 256, 1,024, and 2,048 mounts, and formatting passed. The full gate is still running with no failures reported so far. The scale checks confirm the corrected import-reference costs without growth in candidate or composition work as unrelated mounts increase.

The remaining full-gate work is the populated-store planner regression. No failures have been reported. The next exact run will reuse the completed native42 facts in the dedicated cache; these query fixes require neither a schema change nor fact regeneration.

The final planner test is still active and using CPU; it has not failed or timed out. The scale gate is green. M3 remains gated on the exact #2767 partition, and I’ll launch that diagnostic as soon as this confirmation finishes.

The full gate passed: 5,848/5,848 tests, alongside all three scale campaigns and formatting. The current exact #2767 diagnostic is now running against the dedicated cache. That result is the remaining M2 gate before the atomic Rust production cutover.

The exact run is still in cache startup, carrying the completed native facts forward from schema114 to the current schema115. I’m letting that finish; no cache is being deleted or replaced with an alternate cache. The M3 consumer split and shared graph interface are now recorded in the plan.

Cache startup is actively reading the copied store, with no error reported. I’m leaving it undisturbed. The code and validation receipts are checkpointed; the exact partition and M3 production switch are still outstanding.

Cache startup finished successfully, and the analyzer reused the existing facts without regenerating files. The diagnostic has entered native reverse-query preparation. We can now measure the query fixes against the actual workload.

The native run has selected 1,912 Rust source files across 20 Cargo profiles and is reading the root import facts. I’m keeping the full diagnostic log so any remaining cost or partition failure can be traced to its phase.

Root-fact reads and bridge inventory have completed. The diagnostic is moving through Cargo topology preparation toward the prefix-continuation phase that previously dominated runtime. There is still no final partition result.

The diagnostic has reached module-prefix resolution. The new timers separate that work from prefix continuation, so we can check the indexed fix’s impact without attributing the entire phase to it. I’m monitoring the run while it works toward the exact result.

Module-prefix resolution is still taking substantial time before the continuation stage. I’m checking that phase in parallel while the diagnostic continues. The current test gates are green, but this run still needs to establish the exact partition.

The audit found another concrete source of repeated work: roughly 118,000 distinct positioned prefixes are evaluated one at a time, and each evaluation discards reusable lexical-read artifacts. An Astra worker is extending the existing operation-local artifact cache to these forward queries, with answer, work, and cancellation checks. The current diagnostic continues in parallel.

Continuing. The full 5,848-test gate and all three scale checks are green; the exact diagnostic is still running. In parallel, I’m addressing the additional repeated lexical-read work it exposed, without changing the cache schema or regenerating facts.

An environment failure just interrupted the work: the diagnostic process has disappeared, and Git now reports empty objects and cannot parse `HEAD`. Disk space is available. I’m checking the damage read-only and asking the worker to pause Git writes so we preserve the working files.

The host restarted. I found 12 empty objects in the shared Git database, including branch2771’s current commit; the last verified checkpoint, `9da94665a`, is still readable. The working files are present. I’m preserving them and the damaged Git metadata before any repair.

The host rebooted, killing the exact diagnostic and leaving 12 empty Git objects, including branch2771’s `HEAD`. Working edits are backed up.

5,848 tests and all three scale checks passed; M2’s exact partition and M3 remain unfinished.

May I repair the shared Git metadata, preserve all working changes, and resume?
